name: Gareth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an aluminium extrusion press at a factory that makes window and door frames. We heat aluminium logs, they're called billets, till they're soft, then the press pushes them through a steel die like toothpaste and out comes a long frame profile. I set the die, watch the temperature and the speed, and check the profiles for scratches and twists before they go to the saw. It's hot work and you can't daydream, because a bad billet can jam the whole thing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like away from the press?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Hana, she works in the office at a building supplies firm, and we're hoping to start a family in the next couple of years. We rent a two-bed, and we've got about four months' savings. On Saturdays I coach the under-twelves at the cricket club. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly when Hana makes me, to sort the club's fixtures or write a letter to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to making things. Too much talk, not enough work. I'd say it at the club bar after a match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means our plans stay on track, and that's what matters to me. Kids, maybe a house in a few years. I'd breathe out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the press and ask about the supervisor training, because a steady future means it's worth climbing. We'd try for a baby next year as planned. I'd keep putting about a hundred and fifty a month away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a decent forecast for the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like most about the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Making something people can see. I drive past houses and think, those frames came off my press. My son or daughter will be able to point at a window and say my dad made that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, what would you want the company to do more of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. The company does a few apprenticeships every year, and I'd want more of that. Young lads learning a trade beats them sitting at home on their phones.

S0.say: I'd say good, let's get back to making things, because there's been too much talk and not enough work. I'd say it at the cricket club bar after a match.
S0.think: It means our plans stay on track, with kids and maybe a house in a few years. I'd breathe out.
S0.do: Carries on at the extrusion press and asks about supervisor training. Tries for a baby next year as planned and keeps saving about 150 a month.
S0.feel: Calm, like a decent weekend forecast.
S0.quote: My son or daughter will be able to point at a window and say my dad made that.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth takes pride in making visible things and in coaching young people. His plans revolve around starting a family with Hana. He favours apprenticeships as the route for young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms have to move with the times or they go under, and that's fair. But they should train their own people up before hiring from outside. Apprenticeships, proper ones, not online courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the press itself could run with fewer people. The checking and the handling could go to cameras and robot arms. But someone still needs to set the dies and fix the jams, and I'd want to be that someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the first couple of lads do it, I'd sign up for the company's maintenance apprenticeship, the adult version, two days a week for eighteen months. We'd probably push the baby back a year, just to see how things settle. And I'd save a bit more, maybe two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not lost. It's change I think I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the first couple of lads to do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not the type to jump first. I like to see the new thing work before I put my name down. But I'm not the type to sit still either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana think about pushing the baby back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we're being too careful, she always does. But I'd want to know my job's solid before we have a baby. She'd agree in the end, I think.

S1.say: I'd say firms have to move with the times or go under, which is fair, but they should train their own people first. Proper apprenticeships, not online courses.
S1.think: The checking and handling could go to cameras and robot arms, but someone still needs to set dies and fix jams. I'd want to be that someone.
S1.do: Signs up for the company's adult maintenance apprenticeship, two days a week for eighteen months, once a couple of colleagues have done it. Pushes plans for a baby back a year and saves about 200 a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not lost, confident he can handle the change.
S1.quote: I'm not the type to jump first. I like to see the new thing work before I put my name down.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth accepts automation as fair business but wants firms to train their own. He moves once others have proved the path, not before. Delaying a baby is a real cost he's willing to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and people need time. The government should make the companies keep apprenticeships going and slow things down where it can. I'd say families need to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of work in a year and a bit, and so would Hana, since AI could do her office job too. Two years isn't long enough for anything. We'd have four months of savings and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put the baby off completely, and I'd look straight away for work that might last a bit longer, maybe fitting windows on site with my cousin, because I'd still know the frames. I'd cut the spending right down. If we lost both jobs we'd move in with Hana's parents, who have the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake thinking about what I'd tell Hana's dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana's dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd do anything to keep his daughter looked after. He worked two jobs to put her through college. I wouldn't want to look like I'd failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fitting windows on site might last longer. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe a few months longer. Robots on building sites are harder, everything's different every time. But I really don't know.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and people need time, so government should make companies keep apprenticeships going and slow things down. Families need to pull together.
S2.think: I'd be out of work in a year or so, and so would Hana since AI could do her office job. Four months of savings and that's it.
S2.do: Puts the baby off entirely and looks immediately for work likely to last longer, such as fitting windows with his cousin. Cuts spending sharply and plans to move in with Hana's parents if both lose their jobs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake thinking about what to tell Hana's father.
S2.quote: I'd be lying awake thinking about what I'd tell Hana's dad.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth's alarm comes from the prospect of losing both incomes and from pride about providing. He'd switch to site work quickly but is honest that he doesn't know how long it would last. Family support is his fallback rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train people up if the firms get on with it. Proper apprenticeships, starting now. I'd say it at work and at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd get the maintenance apprenticeship done and have a couple of years of better pay before it lands. That's worth something. After that, I'd be in the same boat as everyone, just with more savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance apprenticeship in the first year, without waiting for the others this time. We'd hold off on the baby till we see how year two looks. I'd save about two hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't wait for others this time. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady picture there was no clock on it. With five years, if I wait a year to see who does well, that's a fifth of the time gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the supervisor training, if they offered it. Climbing a ladder that's going to be taken away doesn't make sense. I'd rather learn to fix the machines.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to train people up if firms get on with proper apprenticeships, starting now. I'd say it at work and at the club.
S3.think: I'd finish the maintenance apprenticeship and have a couple of years of better pay before it lands. After that I'd be in the same boat, just with more savings.
S3.do: Starts the maintenance apprenticeship in year one without waiting for others. Holds off on a baby until he sees how year two looks and saves about 250 a month.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, with something to work towards.
S3.quote: Climbing a ladder that's going to be taken away doesn't make sense.
S3.fieldNote: With a clear deadline Gareth stops waiting for proof, and he explains why. He'd drop the supervisor ladder for maintenance skills. Family plans are on hold until he sees how things look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run, enough to learn a trade and raise a family. Let the firms train people and let families plan. I'd say it at the club bar, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with a maintenance trade and hopefully a couple of kids at school. If the work dries up then, at least I'd have had a decade to save and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd try for a baby next year as planned. I'd do the maintenance apprenticeship once a couple of lads had done it, so starting in year two. And I'd keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month, maybe more after the apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the warning time change the baby decision for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Ten years is long enough for a baby to be at school before it really hits. Two years isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to pass on to your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a trade's a trade, whatever the tools are. My dad fixed lorries, I run a press. Whatever my kids do, I'd want them to work with their hands and their heads.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run, enough to learn a trade and raise a family, so let firms train people and families plan. I'd say it at the club bar.
S4.think: We'd be fine, with me at thirty-seven holding a maintenance trade and maybe a couple of kids at school. If work dries up then, I'd have had a decade to save and plan.
S4.do: Tries for a baby next year as planned and starts the maintenance apprenticeship in year two, after colleagues have done it. Keeps saving about 150 a month, more after the apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, because ten years feels long.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a baby to be at school before it really hits. Two years isn't.
S4.fieldNote: The warning time directly decides Gareth's family plans: a decade means a baby now. He returns to waiting for others before retraining, as in the steady picture. His pride in trades runs through every answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Losing both jobs before we've even started a family, that's the one. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones the companies have to keep running, and time, so a man can learn something new and still provide for his family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what Hana thinks. She's braver than me about all this. She'd say we'll work it out, and she's usually right.

headlineQuote: She'd say we'll work it out, and she's usually right.
portrait: Gareth Ibrahim, 27, runs an aluminium extrusion press making window frames and is married to Hana, who works in a building supplies office. He coaches under-twelves cricket, takes pride in making things people can see, and uses AI only now and then. He accepts automation as fair business but wants firms to train their own people through apprenticeships. Calm if AI fizzles and alarmed by AGI in two years, which would cost both incomes before they start a family, he moves faster with five years' warning and, with ten, would start a family and then retrain in maintenance.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and Hana could both lose their jobs before starting a family.
whatWouldHelp: Real apprenticeships that companies are required to keep running, and enough time to learn something new while still providing for his family.
